name: Aaron Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me what an ordinary workday sounds like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Aaron, 27, a pianist with a master’s in music. I lead a small jazz group, write charts for singers, record keyboard parts and teach at a music centre. My favourite part is when a singer changes the phrasing and the band follows; the tiring part is chasing approvals for a chart after midnight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What kind of financial room do you have?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The music centre and better recording dates pay me well for this field, and I have almost a year of expenses saved. I live with my partner, who has a full-time job, but I pay my share. There are plenty of nearby teaching and studio posts, though I would have to earn one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that AI can tidy the gig list, but it cannot make us hear a singer's breath together. I have no quarrel with a tool that stays in its lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already use AI now and then for rough schedules, so small time savings are believable. The centre contract and studio work feel safe here; I mostly want late payments to stop being normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the music-centre lessons, Friday band nights and keyboard sessions. This winter I'd test a new AI booking checker against my own calendar, verify every date before sharing it, and use it through the first year only if it stops double bookings without exposing pupils' details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. A tool that saves twenty minutes is welcome, and almost a year's expenses in reserve means a cancelled Friday does not change the rent plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually let the software touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let it compare the bookings I entered, not choose who gets a lesson. A wrong date is embarrassing; a leaked pupil record is much worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep saving with almost a year behind you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I save because a musician's busy season can disappear between two school terms. The cushion lets me turn down a recording date that demands rights to everything I play.

say: I would accept **calendar help** while keeping the band’s listening in human hands.
I would tell players a **twenty-minute saving** is useful without changing the music.
think: The **centre contract** and studio work feel secure in this picture.
My **nearly one-year cushion** makes one cancelled Friday manageable.
do: Keep **centre lessons**, Friday band nights and keyboard sessions through the first year.
Test a new **AI booking checker** this winter against my own calendar.
Use it only after **verifying dates** and protecting pupils’ details.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and rent despite occasional late payments.
S0.quote: A wrong date is embarrassing; a leaked pupil record is much worse.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** does not extend to sharing pupils’ private details.
Higher pay and **almost a year saved** give him room to reject bad recording rights.

steps.text: Keep centre lessons, Friday band nights and keyboard sessions
Test new AI booking checker and verify every date before sharing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that quick charts are useful, but singers should know when a machine wrote the backing. I'd ask the musicians' association for clear credit and reuse rules before fees slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chart writing is perhaps a third of my music income, and that is the first piece a producer can replace. I can teach and play. I cannot lose a third of my music income without noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd learn a new AI chart-checking tool on my own drafts, and compare it with a musician's review before using it for paid work. In the first year, if chart orders fall, I'd offer an ear-training class at the centre only if it funds a room and enough students enrol; I'd ask the association to draft a credit rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the invoices, not about touching a new tool. There are other studios nearby, but each has its own musicians waiting for the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your pay comes from writing charts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a full month, charts cover roughly one in three of my paid hours. If half those orders leave, I would notice it in my savings transfer first, not in the rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask musicians to do together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask players to agree that a recorded part needs named credit and permission before it trains a system. One pianist turning down a job will not make a producer change the contract.

say: I would demand clear **credit** when machines write backing charts.
I would ask the **musicians’ association** to set reuse rules before fees slide.
think: Chart writing supplies about **one-third** of my music income.
Other nearby studios have **waiting musicians**, so a quick replacement job is uncertain.
do: Learn a new **AI chart checker** on my own drafts, comparing a musician’s review before paid use.
Offer a paid **ear-training class** if chart orders fall, the centre funds a room and enough students enrol.
Ask the association for **credit rules** during the first year.
feel: I feel **anxious** about chart invoices, though willing to test a proven tool.
S1.quote: I cannot lose a third of my music income without noticing.
fieldNote: He identifies **chart writing** as a sizeable income source exposed before live performance.
His **class proposal** depends on paid room space and enough enrolled students.

steps.text: Learn AI chart checking on own drafts; compare musician review before paid use
Offer paid ear-training class if chart orders fall, centre funds room and students enrol
Ask musicians’ association for recording credit and reuse rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that thinking AGI by 2028 could write and arrange everything we send as files. Player-level robots arrive about 2031 in the card, so live dates and screen work face different clocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A studio could stop paying for my charts and remote keyboard parts quickly. I have savings and local auditions, but those do not make a year's lost income harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I'd put a separate line for charts, keyboard sessions and teaching in my accounts, and save the extra recording fees. In the first year after AGI arrives, if chart orders halve, I'd stop renting the second rehearsal room, ask the centre for paid ear-training hours if it has a room and enrolled students, and audition for a posted teaching vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious because the first loss is work I am proud of, not just paperwork. I can act, but I still have to replace a real third of my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in 2028 before robots can play piano?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Friday band could keep playing until capable robots arrive around 2031, but I cannot live on four Fridays. My written charts can be undercut in 2028 while my hands are still on the keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your savings on a new studio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy a studio to prove I am ready. I would spend at most a term's class fees on equipment after the centre signs for the room and students actually pay.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from capable robots around 2031.
I would tell the band that **file work** faces an earlier shock than live playing.
think: Studios may stop paying for **charts and remote parts** quickly.
A year’s savings cannot replace a **third of income** indefinitely.
do: Protect **cash reserves** by saving recording fees now and dropping the second room if chart orders halve after 2028.
Request paid **centre hours** with a signed room and paying students; cap equipment spending at one term’s collected class fees.
Audition for a posted **teaching vacancy** if chart orders halve after 2028.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing valued work and a significant income share.
S2.quote: My written charts can be undercut in 2028 while my hands are still on the keys.
fieldNote: His **chart income** is vulnerable at the AGI date despite continued live performances.
His **fallbacks** require lost orders, a paid centre room with students and a real posted vacancy.

steps.text: Save extra paid recording fees before 2028
Stop renting second rehearsal room if chart orders halve after 2028
Request centre hours with signed room and paying students; cap equipment at collected term fees
Audition for posted teaching vacancies in first year after 2028 if chart orders halve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre that five years gives us time to test teaching that uses people's ears, not just prepared files. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and capable robots around 2034, so we should revise both the class plan and live contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a good ear-training course by then and keep my band close to its audience. I still cannot assume that a centre will reserve a room or parents will keep paying once software gives instant feedback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'd take a short teaching certificate only if the centre confirms it qualifies me for a paid advanced class. Before 2031 I'd run one eight-week pilot if a room and six paid places are confirmed; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd continue it only if fees cover the room and my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about how much depends on the centre's decisions. The extra years let me ask for proof before I pay for a certificate or print a course book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn during the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the pilot's fees with the room charge, travel and my teaching hours. Six names on a waiting list are not six paid registrations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test whether the new class earns enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my partner to look over the budget, not to pay for the experiment. If the centre cannot confirm the qualification and room, I would keep teaching my current lessons.

say: I would use five years to test **ear-training teaching** with actual learners.
I would prepare for **2031 thinking AGI** and capable robots around 2034.
think: A strong course could replace some **chart fees** if the centre supports it.
Neither room access nor **paid enrolment** is guaranteed.
do: Take a short **teaching certificate** only if the centre confirms it qualifies me for a paid advanced class.
Run an **eight-week pilot** before 2031 only with a room and six paid places.
Continue the **class** after 2031 only if fees cover room and teaching hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a certificate and class depend on the centre’s decisions.
S3.quote: Six names on a waiting list are not six paid registrations.
fieldNote: He requires **written qualification value** before paying for a short teaching certificate.
His **pilot threshold** is six paid places, not informal interest or a free room promise.

steps.text: Take teaching certificate only if centre confirms paid advanced-class qualification
Run eight-week pilot before 2031 if room and six paid places exist
Continue class in first year after 2031 only if fees cover room and teaching hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger pianists to know the bandstand, know their rights and learn how to teach a room. Thinking AGI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 leave time to build all three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be 37 when arrangement work changes and 40 when robot players appear. My savings help, but I still want to be paid for playing, not just for supervising machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the centre lessons and band dates this year and save part of each chart fee. Over the decade I'd earn the teaching certificate only after the centre confirms a paid class, then build that class when enrolment covers costs; in the first year after 2036 I'd keep live bookings and apply for an open teaching post if centre hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough to plan without rushing. I would be less calm if a school asked me to pay for training before it could show me a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a decade let you change about your career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade could let me become a stronger teacher and still spend most Fridays playing. I would choose courses from actual job requirements, not from a list of fashionable tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner if the centre reduced hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner the centre hours and our savings every term. If hours fell, I would apply for posted work nearby before asking my partner to cover my share of rent.

say: I would tell young pianists to build **live skill**, teaching and rights awareness.
I would place **2036 thinking AGI** before capable robots around 2039.
think: At **37**, I may lose chart income before robot pianists appear.
I still want paid **playing**, even with savings and other possible jobs.
do: Keep **centre lessons** and band dates this year, saving from each paid chart fee.
Earn a **teaching certificate** only after the centre confirms a paid class.
Apply for an open **teaching post** after 2036 if centre hours fall.
feel: I feel **calm** enough to plan, while refusing unfunded training.
S4.quote: I would choose courses from actual job requirements, not from a list of fashionable tools.
fieldNote: He uses a long horizon for **verified teaching credentials**, with centre confirmation before tuition.
He would seek **posted local work** if centre hours fall after 2036, preserving his share of rent.

steps.text: Keep centre lessons now and paid live band bookings through first year after 2036
Save part of each paid chart fee while orders continue
Earn teaching certificate only after centre confirms a paid class
Apply for open teaching posts in first year after 2036 if centre hours fall

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a third of my income from charts could shrink before the centre gives me more teaching hours. A paid room for a pilot class, shared credit rules and a real list of school vacancies would help. I can test a tool, but I cannot test a rent payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the experiments musicians are told to make. A course only helps me if it qualifies me for paid work; a room only helps if students turn up and pay.

headlineQuote: A course only helps me if it qualifies me for paid work; a room only helps if students turn up and pay.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old pianist** with a master’s degree, leading a band, writing charts, recording parts and teaching.
His **higher pay** and nearly one year saved buffer risk, while many local posts still require applications or auditions.
He uses **AI occasionally** and tests new tools on his own work before putting pupils’ details or paid charts at risk.
Fast AGI exposes **chart income** before robot players arrive, and he requires funded rooms and real enrolment for teaching plans.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could cut chart work before a paid class replaces the lost income.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **pilot room** and enough enrolled students would let him test ear-training teaching.
Shared **credit rules** and actual school vacancy lists would support a fair job search.
